item.semiconductor-lab.marine_chronomete: A clock that keeps time even on a rolling ship. It carries the home port's (Greenwich) time so you can find your longitude.

4 bronze + crown glass + 2 crucible steel (mainspring) + ruby boule (jewel bearings) + standard screw. Right-click for Greenwich time and days since it was set. Hold it in the other hand when taking a noon sight with the sextant: longitude = (12:00 - time of noon) x 15 deg. Each one gains or loses a little every day (1 s of error = 15 arcsec of longitude).

In 1707 a British fleet lost its position in fog and ran aground with great loss of life. In 1714 Britain offered a prize for finding longitude. John Harrison, a carpenter by training, spent 40 years on his clocks, and on the 1761 voyage H4 lost only about 5 seconds in 81 days.

The Earth turns 15 deg an hour, so the gap between local noon and Greenwich time is your longitude. Pendulum clocks fail on a rolling ship, so H4 ran on a balance and mainspring compensated so heat would not change it. Its bearings used jewels such as ruby.
Approximation: the daily rate is a game value within +-0.5 s (a game day is 20 minutes).
Aluminium with a little copper and magnesium mixed in.
6 aluminium + copper + magnesium -> 6. Fired in a furnace it becomes quenched duralumin.
Duralumin is aluminium with about 4% Cu, about 0.5% Mg and some Mn.
The name comes from the German town of Düren and aluminium.
Approximation: the proportions are game values (real: about 4% Cu, 0.5% Mg).
item.semiconductor-lab.quenched_duralumi: Duralumin just heated and cooled fast, still soft. Carry it and it slowly hardens.
Duralumin charge in a furnace. After one (game) day in your inventory it turns into hard duralumin (not in chests). Right-click for its current hardness.
In 1906 Alfred Wilm in Germany left a quenched alloy over a weekend and found it had hardened (age hardening).
Quenching traps copper dissolved in the aluminium; even at room temperature copper atoms slowly gather into tiny precipitates that block deformation and harden the metal.
Approximation: about 4 days really; one day in the game, and only in your inventory.

item.semiconductor-lab.duralumin.note1: An aluminium alloy that is light yet nearly as strong as steel. It framed airships and aircraft.
item.semiconductor-lab.duralumin.note2: Quenched duralumin left in your inventory for a day age-hardens into this.
item.semiconductor-lab.duralumin.note3: It framed Zeppelin airships and metal aircraft from the 1910s. Related alloys still skin aircraft today.
item.semiconductor-lab.duralumin.note4: Density about 2.8 g/cm3, about a third of steel (7.9), so its strength per weight is high.
block.semiconductor-lab.conveyor_belt.no: A rubber belt that carries things. Hooked to a drive, items move one block per second.
Crafting: 3 vulcanised rubber + 2 iron → 6. Items move away from the player who placed it (turn it to make corners). One stack per block, shown on top. Right-click with an empty hand to take it.
It does not move by itself. Lay belts beside a conveyor drive, pointing away from it. Up to 64 blocks.
In 1913 Ford's Highland Park plant put car assembly on a moving line, cutting assembly time from about 12 hours to about 1.5 hours ⚠️. Meat-packing overhead lines were said to be the inspiration.
block.semiconductor-lab.conveyor_belt.ho: Lay beside a drive, pointing away from it (items move away from whoever placed it). One block per second, one stack per block.
block.semiconductor-lab.conveyor_drive.n: The motor head that moves a belt. Takes items from the machine behind and feeds the machine at the end.

Crafting: 4 iron + electric motor + copper cable. Takes a stack from the output of the machine behind (opposite the belt), moves the belt one block per second and inserts into the machine past the end. 5 W per belt block.
Hoppers only link neighbours; a belt reaches distant machines. Works with chests too.
No redstone. Runs only while powered.
block.semiconductor-lab.conveyor_drive.p: Omitted: ⚠️ 5 W per belt block is a rough figure. Items hop block to block rather than gliding.
block.semiconductor-lab.conveyor_drive.h: Machine to take from behind, belts beside it pointing away, machine to feed past the end. 5 W per belt block; one block per second.
block.semiconductor-lab.oht_drive.note1: The head of the rail. When the load port below fills its FOUP, it lifts it and carries it to the load port at the end of the rail.
block.semiconductor-lab.oht_drive.note2: Crafting: 2 steel + electric motor + 2 vulcanised rubber + copper cable. When the output FOUP of the load port below (up to 4 blocks) is full at 25, or its input FOUP is empty and the tool has stopped, it carries it to the empty input slot of the load port under a dead end of the rail. 200 W.
block.semiconductor-lab.oht_drive.note3: Travel time grows with rail length (0.25 s per block ⚠️). With several dead ends, it picks the nearest free one.
block.semiconductor-lab.oht_drive.note4: No redstone. Runs only while powered.
block.semiconductor-lab.oht_drive.placeh: Omitted: ⚠️ no carriage is drawn, the rail just glows. Real carriages lower the FOUP on belts. Speed and power are rough.
block.semiconductor-lab.oht_drive.howto: Place up to 4 blocks above a load port and run ceiling rail to above another load port. A full output FOUP goes to the input slot there. 200 W.
gui.semiconductor-lab.oht_drive.no_dest: No free input slot to drop at
A needle that always points north. Hold it to see an arrow to north.
Iron nugget + lodestone + bowl + water bucket (bucket returns). A needle rubbed on a lodestone floats on water. Iron or steel blocks nearby throw it off.
Around 1088 the Chinese scholar Shen Kuo described finding direction with a magnetised needle. Ships used it by the 12th century.

The Earth is a big magnet and the needle lines up with its field. On iron ships the hull pulled the needle, so Flinders (about 1801) used an iron bar and Kelvin (1876) iron balls to cancel it. ⚠️ Declination (true vs magnetic north) is skipped.
Approximation: declination is skipped; the pull of iron is a game value.
